1422.title: The schools you met
1422.hook: which way of practice drew you?
1422.howItsDone: People who explore several practices often keep a notebook of what drew them and why, then look for a teacher or a community in the tradition that keeps that practice, and learn from them as a guest.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was what science taught: attention, habit and compassion can grow, modestly, and the studies say so with care. Your line was it grew.

A cushion in a Zen hall, facing a plain wall. Beads moving through fingers, one name at a time. A man alone in a field at night, talking to God in his own words. A room of Quakers, quiet until someone is moved to speak. People in a park, moving slowly through the morning air. A table of Jewish students arguing over one line of text. This year, the path toured the world's schools of practice, each on its own terms. Today, one question over the whole road. Not which way is best. Which way, if any, drew you?
screen: `A WALL, A BEAD, A FIELD AT NIGHT.` → `ONE SCHOOL AT A TIME.` → `WHICH WAY DREW YOU?`

segments.voice: First, a pull is not a ranking. The schools aim at different ends: some at God, some at awakening, some at character, some at calm. Being drawn to a Zen wall says nothing against a Sufi circle. It says something about you, today. Second, a pull is a place to start, not a proof. In his first letter to the Thessalonians, Paul writes: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Christians read that line in its own setting, inside the life of a church. Taken plainly, it holds two moves: test first, then keep. Zen, Tibetan Buddhism and some Hindu paths, as this path met them, stressed the teacher: a tug is where you start, and a good teacher and a community help you test it. Third, a pull is an invitation, not a purchase. Some of what you met belongs inside a faith and its people. The Jesus Prayer lives in the prayer life of Orthodox Christians. The Mevlevi turning is, for those who keep it, a ceremony of remembrance, not a performance. A pull toward one is an invitation to learn from its keepers, as a guest. Fourth, name the why. The what is a practice; the why is a need. Someone drawn to Quaker silence might be hungry for rest; someone drawn to kirtan, for company. A need can travel with you even when a practice can't, and naming it makes the next step easier to see.
screen: `A PULL IS NOT A RANKING.` · `PROVE, THEN HOLD FAST.` · `AN INVITATION, NOT A PURCHASE.` · `THE WHY IS A NEED.` · then, large: `DRAWN TO.`

segments.voice: Let the tour pass by like a slow train: the wall, the beads, the field, the silent room, the park, the study table, and notice which one stays in the window a moment longer; if none does, that's fine too. If one does, ask quietly what in it pulls, the silence, the body moving, the words, the people. If you pray, you can bring the question into prayer.
The schools you met. Zen and insight, Tibetan, Christian, Jewish, Muslim and Sufi, Hindu, Sikh, Chinese and modern ways, each met in its own words and never ranked. Today's word.
Your line: drawn to. A pull is a beginning, never a verdict on anyone else's way. See you tomorrow.

1423.title: What doesn't fit
1423.hook: some things you met aren't for you
1423.howItsDone: People who try several practices may set some aside; doing it respectfully means not mocking the practice, and giving thanks for what it showed them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the schools you met, and the question was which way of practice drew you, and why. Your line was drawn to.

A book a friend lent you, its spine soft from years of rereading. They pressed it into your hands because it changed something for them. You've opened it again and again, and it won't open for you. You don't throw it away. You don't tell your friend it's a bad book. You hand it back, and say thank you. Yesterday asked what drew you. Today is the other half. Some of what you met this year may not be for you: a chant that sounded like someone else's song, a sit that never opened, a thinker whose pages stayed shut. Today is about handing those back, kindly.
screen: `A BOOK THAT WON'T OPEN.` → `HAND IT BACK, WITH THANKS.` → `THE OTHER HALF OF THE LOOK BACK.`

segments.voice: First, not for me is not the same as not good. A practice that doesn't fit you is still whole for the people who keep it. A dawn prayer, a string of beads, a koan, an hour of silence: some people build their lives around each. Not for me is a sentence about me. It says nothing about the practice. Second, a teacher's picture. In The Prophet, Kahlil Gibran writes about what a real teacher does: "If he is indeed wise he does not bid you enter the house of his wisdom, but rather leads you to the threshold of your own mind." This year brought you to a great many houses. Not every one was meant to be moved into. Some were meant to be visited, admired and left, the door closed gently behind you. Third, not for me can also mean not now. A book that won't open at one time of life sometimes opens at another. Letting something go kindly leaves the door unlocked. Letting it go with a sneer bolts it shut. Fourth, how to let go well. No mocking, no little story about how silly it was. Name one thing it taught you, even if it's only what you don't need; a practice you set down can still teach you something true about yourself. That's the thank-you note tucked inside the cover.

Ask what it taught you, even a little, then set it down in your mind, like a borrowed book handed back. If you pray, you can give thanks for the people who keep it.

1424.title: Your practice so far
1424.howItsDone: People who keep a personal spiritual practice often take stock at the end of a season by writing down what they actually do each day and week, rather than what they hope to do, and build from that list.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was what doesn't fit: a borrowed book, handed back with thanks. Your line was not for me.

One question, quick to ask and harder than it sounds. Not what practice you admire. Not what you plan to start on Monday. What did you actually do yesterday that you'd call practice? A breath before a meal. A line said under your breath. A slow walk. A pause before a sharp reply. This path has handed you pieces for four years, and this year alone brought Tao Te Ching chapters, Montaigne's attempts, Thoreau's woods and a tour of the world's schools. Some pieces stuck. Some went back in the box. Today is an inventory, with one rule: only what you actually do.
screen: `WHAT DID YOU ACTUALLY DO?` → `FOUR YEARS OF PIECES.` → `ONE RULE: ONLY WHAT YOU DO.`

segments.voice: First, admired is not the same as done. A shelf can hold books you meant to read, and a mind can hold practices you meant to keep. That's not a failing. The admired list is a wish; the done list is a map, and you can only start a trip from where you really are. Second, an old check. This year brought Zengzi, a student of Confucius, who in the Analects examines himself every day on three points. Had he been loyal in working for others? Trustworthy with friends? And the third: had he practiced what he was taught? Not learned. Practiced. The Analects puts the weight on doing. Third, small counts. In the book of Zechariah, in a passage about a building just begun, the prophet asks: "For who hath despised the day of small things?" A practice that has become habit can be so quiet you forget to list it: the breath before you answer, the cup of tea drunk slowly on purpose, the walk without your phone. Those belong on the list. Fourth, a short list is an honest list. If what you actually do fits on one line, that line is worth more than a page of plans. It's real, it's yours, and it already works in your life. Tomorrow looks ahead. Today, only the ground under your feet.
screen: `ADMIRED IS NOT THE SAME AS DONE.` · `ZENGZI: DID I PRACTICE IT?` · `SMALL COUNTS.` · `A SHORT LIST IS AN HONEST LIST.` · then, large: `WHAT I DO.`

segments.voice: Walk back through yesterday slowly, from waking to sleep, like rewinding a film, and each time you meet something you'd call practice, a pause, a prayer, a walk, a kind word said on purpose, note it and keep going. Leave off the things you only meant to do, and if the list is short, let it be short. If you pray, put prayer on the list exactly as it really happens.
Your practice so far. Not the practices you admire, but the ones you actually do, gathered from four years of pieces. Today's word.
Your line: what I do. However short, it's the ground everything else will stand on. Same time tomorrow.

1425.title: Ahead: the summit
1425.hook: year five reads the source texts slowly and builds your own lasting practice
1425.howItsDone: People following a long course of study often pause before its final stage to look at what's ahead and choose one practice they mean to keep through to the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was your practice so far: an inventory with one rule, only what you actually do. Your line was what I do.

Near the top of a mountain, the trail changes. The trees thin out. The steps get steeper and slower. And for the first time on the whole climb, you can turn around and see the valley you came from: the switchbacks, the stream you crossed, the place you nearly turned back. Then you turn again and look up. The top is close enough to see now, and still not close enough to touch. The day after tomorrow, this path begins its fifth year, and the outline has a name for that year: the summit. Today is a look up the slope before the last climb.
screen: `THE TREES THIN OUT.` → `LOOK BACK AT THE VALLEY.` → `THEN LOOK UP.`

segments.voice: First, reading the sources slowly. Year five opens with short sacred texts read whole: the Dhammapada, the Psalms, the Sermon on the Mount, the Bhagavad Gita, the Quran, the Japji of Guru Nanak, the Heart Sutra, the Analects, Ecclesiastes and more. Each belongs first to the people who keep it, so the year begins by learning to read as a guest. Second, walking with the poets: Rumi again, Hafiz and Kabir, Tagore, haiku, George Herbert, Hopkins, Wordsworth and Blake, Whitman, Dickinson. Not a survey. Companions for the walk. Third, building your own practice. The year turns from reading to making: a daily practice, a weekly one, the seasons of a year and of a life, what to do when it breaks, and at the end, writing your own rule. That's where yesterday's honest list comes in. You build from what you already do, not from a wish. Fourth, a line from the end of Walden. Henry David Thoreau wrote: "If you have built castles in the air, your work need not be lost; that is where they should be. Now put the foundations under them." Four years of thinkers, questions and schools have built a good many castles in the air. Thoreau doesn't ask you to knock them down. He asks for foundations. And a summit isn't where the mountain ends. You still walk down. What changes is the view you carry with you.
screen: `READING THE SOURCES SLOWLY.` · `WALKING WITH THE POETS.` · `BUILDING YOUR OWN PRACTICE.` · `THOREAU: FOUNDATIONS UNDER CASTLES.` · then, large: `THE SUMMIT.`

segments.voice: Bring yesterday's list to mind and look at it the way a climber looks back at the valley: this is how far it came. Then, gently, look up, with no plans and no promises, and ask one quiet question: which of these would I like to carry all the way to the top? Let one rise a little above the rest, and if you pray, you can hold it in prayer.
Ahead. The year in front of you: the sources read slowly, the poets as companions, and a lasting practice of your own, built on foundations. Today's word.
Your line: the summit. Two days from now, the last climb begins. See you on the slope.

1426.title: Year four close
1426.hook: a year with thinkers and schools
1426.howItsDone: Some people close a year of study with a slow walk, recalling what they read and choosing one line to carry into the next year; some traditions keep a walking meditation of their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ahead: the sources read slowly, the poets, a practice of your own. Your line was the summit.

Like water. My attempt. Look as if for the first time. Go to the woods. Solid and light. Thank you. Those lines closed each stretch of this year: the Tao Te Ching, Montaigne, Emerson, Thoreau, the science, and the tour of the world's schools. Read in a row, they sound less like conclusions and more like directions for a walk. Soften. Try. Look. Get outside. Keep what's sure, hold the rest loosely. Say thank you on the way out. Today the year ends, and the first book it opened has one more word for the road.
screen: `LIKE WATER. MY ATTEMPT. LOOK.` → `THE WOODS. SOLID AND LIGHT. THANK YOU.` → `DIRECTIONS FOR A WALK.`

segments.voice: First, four companions, read slowly. Lao Tzu, whose book begins by admitting that words fall short. Montaigne, who wrote about himself in pieces he called attempts. Emerson, who asked readers to look as if for the first time. Thoreau, who went to live by a pond to see what life had to teach. None of them asked to be obeyed. Each walked beside you for a while, then let you go. Second, science, told honestly. Attention, habit and compassion can grow, the studies said, modestly. So the year's rule was simple: keep what's solid, hold the rest lightly. Third, the world's schools, never ranked: Zen halls and Sufi circles, Jewish study pairs and Quaker silence, Hindu chant and Sikh dawn prayer, Chinese parks at sunrise, each met in its own words. This last week asked what drew you, what doesn't fit, and what you actually do. Fourth, water, one more time. The Tao Te Ching, in its eighth chapter, says the highest good is like water. Water benefits everything and doesn't contend. It settles in the low places people look down on. Elsewhere the book adds that nothing is softer than water, yet nothing does better against what is hard. Watch any stream: the water doesn't fight the stone; it goes around. The year's first book gives a fair picture of how to walk out of it: not racing to the top, not standing still, but moving on, steadily and low.

segments.voice: If you can stand and move, walk a room or a hallway at half your usual speed, letting your path bend around what's there, a chair, a doorframe, a corner, without pushing anything aside, and letting each step settle before the next. If walking isn't possible, let your breath move like water instead, never forced, or trace a slow, winding path with one hand. Nowhere to arrive; if you pray, you can walk with a prayer.
Year four close. A year with thinkers and schools: four companions read slowly, science told honestly, and the world's ways of practice, each in its own words. Today's word.
Your line: on toward the top. Year five begins tomorrow, reading as a guest. That's year four, complete.

1427.title: Reading as a guest
1427.hook: a sacred text belongs first to the people who pray it; read with that respect
1427.tomorrow: why would anyone read the same three lines three times?
1427.howItsDone: Some readers outside a tradition start a sacred text by asking someone who prays it how their community reads it, and by reading a commentary from inside that tradition before forming their own view.

segments.voice: Yesterday, year four closed on water: steady and low, going around the stone. On toward the top. Year five opens with a book in your hands that belongs to someone else.

At a friend's family wedding, the band plays a song half the room has streamed for the beat. Then the groom's grandmother starts crying at the second verse. It was sung at her own wedding, in a language most of the room doesn't speak. Same song. The room knew the tune; she knows what it's for. Year five opens old books, starting soon with the Dhammapada, and every one of them has a grandmother like that. So, one question for today: how do you read a book that belongs to someone else's family?
screen: `A SONG FOR THE BEAT.` → `A GRANDMOTHER IN TEARS.` → `WHOSE BOOK IS IT?`

segments.voice: This path has no scripture of its own. So every holy book it opens belongs first to the people who pray it, sing it, read it over their dead. That makes the reader here a guest. And guests are an old subject. In Genesis, Abraham sits at his tent door in the heat of the day, sees three men, and runs to meet them. He bows and says, "Let a little water, I pray you, be fetched, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree." Then bread, and a meal. Later in the Torah, welcome becomes a command. Leviticus says, "the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." That's what this path shares with its Jewish neighbor: care for how guest and host treat each other. And the honest difference: in the Torah, the welcome is a commandment, with a people's memory behind it. Here, reading as a guest is a manner you choose, and nothing commands it. What does the manner look like? A guest asks how the hosts read the book before deciding what a line means. A guest says "Buddhists read this as", not "this really means". A guest never takes a line to use against the people it belongs to. And a guest can be moved to tears and still be a guest.

segments.voice: A short note from someone who matters often gets read more than once. The first time, for what it says. The second time, slower, one word stands out. By the third, the reading has turned into something else: staying with it. So, yesterday's question: why would anyone read the same three lines three times? Augustine tells his own story about what a few lines can do.
screen: `A SHORT NOTE.` → `WHAT IT SAYS. ONE WORD. STAYING.` → `A PAGE CAN DO IT TOO.`

segments.voice: In his Confessions, Augustine sits in a garden in Milan, weeping, stuck between the life he has and the one he wants. From a house nearby he hears a child's voice chanting, "Take up and read; Take up and read." He picks up the apostle Paul's letters, reads the first passage his eyes fall on, a few lines, and stops. In his words: "No further would I read; nor needed I." A few lines were enough. Christian monks kept a practice of reading like that and called it lectio divina, holy reading. The Rule of Saint Benedict sets hours of the monk's day aside for it. A Carthusian monk named Guigo drew it as a ladder with four rungs: reading, meditation, prayer, contemplation. His picture is a meal. Reading puts the food in your mouth. Meditation chews it. Prayer tastes it. Contemplation is the sweetness itself. Some groups who practice it today read one short passage aloud three times, with silence after each. The first reading is for what it says. The second is for one word or phrase that stands out. The third is for staying with that word. Then the reading stops, and the quiet does the rest. A guest at that table can borrow the pace without claiming the prayer. Three times.
